Boundedness in a two-dimensional chemotaxis-haptotaxis system

Youshan Tao Note: taoys@dhu.edu.cn Affiliation: Department of Applied Mathematics, Dong Hua University, Affiliation: Shanghai 200051, P.R. China
Abstract

This work studies the chemotaxis-haptotaxis system

{ut=Δu−χ∇⋅(u∇v)−ξ∇⋅(u∇w)+μu(1−u−w),x∈Ω,t>0,vt=Δ​v−v+u,x∈Ω,t>0,wt=−v​w,x∈Ω,t>0,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}u_{t}=\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)-\xi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla w)+\mu u(1-u-w),&\qquad x\in\Omega,\,t>0,\\[2.84526pt] v_{t}=\Delta v-v+u,&\qquad x\in\Omega,\,t>0,\\[2.84526pt] w_{t}=-vw,&\qquad x\in\Omega,\,t>0,\end{array}\right.

in a bounded smooth domain Ω⊂ℝ2\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} with zero-flux boundary conditions, where the parameters χ,ξ\chi,\xi and μ\mu are assumed to be positive. It is shown that under appropriate regularity assumption on the initial data (u0,v0,w0)(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0}), the corresponding initial-boundary problem possesses a unique classical solution which is global in time and bounded. In addition to coupled estimate techniques, a novel ingredient in the proof is to establish a one-sided pointwise estimate, which connects Δ​w\Delta w to vv and thereby enables us to derive useful energy-type inequalities that bypass ww. However, we note that the approach developed in this paper seems to be confined to the two-dimensional setting.
Key words: chemotaxis, haptotaxis, logistic source, boundedness, coupled estimates
AMS Classification: 35A01, 35B40, 35B65, 35K57, 35Q92, 92C17

1 Introduction

1.1 Chemotaxis-haptotaxis model

We consider the chemotaxis-haptotaxis system

{ut=Δu−χ∇⋅(u∇v)−ξ∇⋅(u∇w)+μu(1−u−w),x∈Ω,t>0,vt=Δ​v−v+u,x∈Ω,t>0,wt=−v​w,x∈Ω,t>0,\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}u_{t}=\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)-\xi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla w)+\mu u(1-u-w),&\qquad x\in\Omega,\,t>0,\\[2.84526pt] v_{t}=\Delta v-v+u,&\qquad x\in\Omega,\,t>0,\\[2.84526pt] w_{t}=-vw,&\qquad x\in\Omega,\,t>0,\end{array}\right. (1.1)

in a physical smoothly bounded domain Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}, n∈{2,3}n\in\{2,3\}, under zero-flux boundary conditions

∂u∂ν−χ​u​∂v∂ν−ξ​u​∂w∂ν=∂v∂ν=0,x∈∂Ω,t>0\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}-\chi u\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}-\xi u\frac{\partial w}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}=0,\qquad x\in\partial\Omega,\,t>0 (1.2)

and with prescribed initial data

u⁡(x,0)=u0​(x),v⁡(x,0)=v0​(x),w⁡(x,0)=w0​(x),x∈Ω,u(x,0)=u_{0}(x),\quad v(x,0)=v_{0}(x),\quad w(x,0)=w_{0}(x),\qquad x\in\Omega, (1.3)

where ∂∂ν\frac{\partial}{\partial\nu} denotes differentiation with respect to outward normal on ∂Ω\partial\Omega, and the parameters χ,ξ\chi,\xi and μ\mu are assumed to be positive. This system was initially proposed by Chaplain and Lolas [3, 4] to model the process of cancer cell invasion of surrounding tissue. In this context, uu represents the density of cancer cell, vv denotes the concentration of enzyme, and ww stands for the density of extracellular matrix (tissue). In addition to random motion, cancer cells bias their movement towards a gradient of diffusible enzyme as well as a gradient of non-diffusible tissue by detecting matrix molecules such as vitronectin adhered therein. We refer to the aforementioned two directed migrations of cancer cells as chemotaxis and haptotaxis, respectively. The cancer cells are also assumed to undergo birth and death in a logistic manner, competing for space with healthy tissue. The enzyme is produced by cancer cells, and it is supposed to be influenced by diffusion and degradation. The tissue is stiff in the sense that it does not diffuse, but it could be degraded by enzyme upon contact.

1.2 Previous related works on global well-posedness

When w≡0w\equiv 0, the PDE system (1.1) is reduced to the chemotaxis-only system

{ut=Δu−χ∇⋅(u∇v)+μu(1−u),x∈Ω,t>0,vt=Δ​v−v+u,x∈Ω,t>0.\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}u_{t}=\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)+\mu u(1-u),&\qquad x\in\Omega,\,t>0,\\[2.84526pt] v_{t}=\Delta v-v+u,&\qquad x\in\Omega,\,t>0.\end{array}\right.

This system has been widely studied. In the case μ=0\mu=0, solutions may blow up in finite time when n≥2n\geq 2 [7, 13, 24]; however, it is known that arbitrarily small μ>0\mu>0 guarantee the global existence and boundedness of solutions when n=2n=2 [14], and that appropriately large μχ\frac{\mu}{\chi} preclude blow-up in the case n≥3n\geq 3 [22]. Very recently, it is asserted that sufficiently large μχ\frac{\mu}{\chi} enforce the stability of constant equilibria [25].
When χ=0\chi=0, the PDE system (1.1) becomes the haptotaxis-only system

{ut=Δu−ξ∇⋅(u∇w)+μu(1−u−w),x∈Ω,t>0,vt=Δ​v−v+u,x∈Ω,t>0,wt=−v​w,x∈Ω,t>0.\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}u_{t}=\Delta u-\xi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla w)+\mu u(1-u-w),&\qquad x\in\Omega,\,t>0,\\[2.84526pt] v_{t}=\Delta v-v+u,&\qquad x\in\Omega,\,t>0,\\[2.84526pt] w_{t}=-vw,&\qquad x\in\Omega,\,t>0.\end{array}\right.

Global existence theories for this system were explored in [5, 6, 21], whereas the boundedness and asymptotic behavior of solution was studied in [11]. The above results rule out the possibility of blow-up of solutions to this haptotaxis-only system, although the solutions may exhibit some pattern for certain ranges of model parameters and initial data [4].
Compared with the chemotaxis-only system and the haptotaxis-only system, the coupled chemotaxis-haptotaxis system (1.1) is much less understood. As far as we know, when n∈{2,3}n\in\{2,3\}, the global boundedness of solutions for this system has remained pending so far, although the global existence was examined in [15, 16]. The purpose of this work is to answer this issue of boundedness when n=2n=2.

1.3 Main results

As to the above initial data we suppose that for some α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) we have

{u0∈C0​(Ω¯)withu0≥0in ​Ωandu0≢0,v0∈W1,∞​(Ω)withv0≥0in ​Ω,w0∈C2+α​(Ω¯)withw0>0in ​Ω¯with∂w0∂ν=0on ​∂Ω.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}u_{0}\in C^{0}(\overline{\Omega})\quad\mbox{with}\quad u_{0}\geq 0\quad\mbox{in }\Omega\quad\mbox{and}\quad u_{0}\not\equiv 0,\\[2.84526pt] v_{0}\in W^{1,\infty}(\Omega)\quad\mbox{with}\quad v_{0}\geq 0\quad\mbox{in }\Omega,\\[2.84526pt] w_{0}\in C^{2+\alpha}(\overline{\Omega})\quad\mbox{with}\quad w_{0}>0\quad\mbox{in }\overline{\Omega}\quad\mbox{with}\quad\frac{\partial w_{0}}{\partial\nu}=0\quad\mbox{on }\partial\Omega.\end{array}\right. (1.6)

Under these assumptions, our main result reads as follows.

Theorem 1.1

Let n=2n=2, and suppose that χ>0\chi>0, ξ>0\xi>0 and μ>0\mu>0. Then for each (u0,v0,w0)(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0}) fulfilling (1.6), (1.1)-(1.3) possesses a unique classical solution which is global in time and bounded in Ω×(0,∞)\Omega\times(0,\infty).

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first boundedness result addressing the full parabolic-parabolic-ODE chemotaxis-haptotaxis model, despite there exist some boundedness and stabilization results on the simplified parabolic-elliptic-ODE chemotaxis-haptotaxis model in which the spatiotemporal evolution of chemical concentration is described by the elliptic equation 0=Δ​v−v+u0=\Delta v-v+u replacing the original parabolic counterpart ([19, 20]). Here we should point out that the full chemotaxis-haptotaxis system is much more mathematically challenging than the aforementioned simplified one.

1.4 Approaches used in the paper

A main technical difficulty in the proof of Theorem 1.1 emanates from consequences of the strong coupling in (1.1) on the spatial regularity of uu, vv and ww. Another analytical obstacle stems from the fact that a bound of ∇v\nabla v in Lp​(Ω)L^{p}(\Omega) cannot leads to a time-independent bound for ∇w\nabla w in Lp​(Ω)L^{p}(\Omega), because

∇w(x,t)=∇w0(x)e−∫0tv(x,s)ds−w0(x)e−∫0tv(x,s)ds∫0t∇v(x,s)ds\displaystyle\nabla w(x,t)=\nabla w_{0}(x)\,e^{-\int_{0}^{t}v(x,s)ds}-w_{0}(x)\,e^{-\int_{0}^{t}v(x,s)ds}\,\int_{0}^{t}\nabla v(x,s)ds

in which the last term ∫0t∇v​(x,s)​𝑑s\int_{0}^{t}\nabla v(x,s)ds is non-local in time. It will be crucial to our approach to build a one-sided pointwise estimate which connects Δ​w\Delta w to vv (see Lemma 2.2 below). Relying on such a pointwise estimate, we can derive two useful energy-type inequalities that bypass ww (see Lemmata 2.3 and 3.3 below). Using such information along with coupled estimate techniques, we establish estimates on ∫Ωu2+∫Ω|∇v|4\int_{\Omega}u^{2}+\int_{\Omega}|\nabla v|^{4} and ∫Ωup\int_{\Omega}u^{p} for any p>2p>2, which results in the boundedness of uu in L∞​(Ω)L^{\infty}(\Omega) by performing the Moser iteration procedure (see Lemmata 3.8, 3.10 and 4.1 below).
Finally, we mention that the methods developed in this paper are restricted to the two-dimensional setting, and thus the boundedness for the corresponding three-dimensional problem largely remains open.

The following basic property on mass can be easily checked.

Lemma 2.4

The solution (u,v,w)(u,v,w) of (1.1)-(1.3) fulfills

∫Ωu⁡(x,t)​𝑑x\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}u(x,t)dx ≤\displaystyle\leq m∗:=max⁡{|Ω|,∫Ωu0​(x)​𝑑x}for all ​t∈(0,Tm​a​x).\displaystyle m^{*}:=\max\Big\{|\Omega|,\int_{\Omega}u_{0}(x)dx\Big\}\qquad\mbox{for all }t\in(0,T_{max}). (2.16)

Proof.  We integrate the first equation in (1.1) with respect to space to obtain

In order to establish a bound of uu in L∞​(Ω)L^{\infty}(\Omega), we first build an estimate on ∫Ωu​ln⁡u\int_{\Omega}u\ln u as a starting point of our reasoning, which heavily depends on the pointwise estimate (2.6) for −Δ​w-\Delta w.

4 Boundedness. Proof of Theorem 1.1

Although (3.33) shows that ∇v​(⋅,t)\nabla v(\cdot,t) is bounded in L∞​(Ω)L^{\infty}(\Omega), ∇w​(⋅,t)\nabla w(\cdot,t) might become unbounded in L∞​(Ω)L^{\infty}(\Omega) in light of (2.4). Therefore, we cannot directly apply the result of the well-known Moser-Alikakos iteration [1] to the first equation in (1.1) to gain the boundedness of u⁡(⋅,t)u(\cdot,t) in L∞​(Ω)L^{\infty}(\Omega). To bypass ww, our strategy is to use (2.11) as a starting point for our proof.

We are now in a position to prove Theorem 1.1.
Proof of Theorem 1.1.  The statement of global classical solvability and boundedness is a straightforward consequence of Lemma 2.1 and Lemma 4.1. □\Box
